desc:
Each segment [start, end] covers every integer position from start to end inclusive. For every value x in points, report how many segments cover position x.

Return the answers in the same order as points.

segments = [[1, 4], [3, 6], [4, 4]], points = [4, 0, 5, 7]
result = [3, 0, 1, 0]

Position 4 lies in all three segments, 0 and 7 lie in none, and 5 lies only in [3, 6].
hints: Checking every segment for every point costs O(segments × points), which is far too slow at 100,000 each.
The coverage count at position x only changes where a segment starts (+1) or has just ended (-1). Record those changes once, then answer all points from one table.
Keep diff[start] += 1 and diff[end + 1] -= 1 on an array of size 100,002. A running prefix sum gives cover[x] for every position, and each point is then a lookup.
editorial: This is the difference array applied to counting. Let cover[x] be the number of segments containing x. A segment adds 1 on start..end, which changes the difference cover[x] - cover[x - 1] only at start (+1) and at end + 1 (-1).

Fill the difference array in O(segments), prefix-sum it once in O(R) where R = 100,001 is the coordinate range, then answer each point in O(1). Total time O(R + segments + points), space O(R). If coordinates were huge you would compress them or sort the starts and ends and use binary search instead.
solution:
def coverageAtPoints(segments, points):
    size = 100002
    diff = [0] * (size + 1)
    for start, end in segments:
        diff[start] += 1
        diff[end + 1] -= 1
    cover = [0] * size
    run = 0
    for x in range(size):
        run += diff[x]
        cover[x] = run
    return [cover[x] for x in points]
